content: All vaccines must be administered strictly according to the guidelines provided in the product label or package insert. The section on vaccine selection lists all vaccines that are licensed by the USDA and available in the United States at the time of publication. Any new vaccine approvals or changes to label specifications that occur after publication should also be considered part of this list. Any of the listed vaccines may be used for revaccination, even if the brand differs from the one previously administered. Vaccines used in state and local rabies control programs should provide immunity for a duration of three years, as this is the most effective way to increase the proportion of immunized dogs and cats in a population. There is no laboratory or epidemiological evidence to support the annual or biennial administration of three-year vaccines after the initial series. Currently, there is no epidemiological evidence linking any specific licensed vaccine product to adverse events, including vaccine failure. Any adverse events should be reported to the vaccine manufacturer and to the USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), Center for Veterinary Biologics. Reports can be submitted online, by telephone, or via email. The efficacy of rabies vaccination in wildlife and hybrid animals (offspring of wild animals crossbred with domestic animals) has not been established, and no vaccine is licensed for use in these animals. These guidelines, along with information on the local and regional status of animal rabies and the availability of human rabies biologics, can be obtained from state health departments. Rabies vaccinations may also be administered to animals in animal control shelters under the supervision of a veterinarian before their release. Within 28 days of the primary vaccination, the animal achieves a peak rabies antibody titer and is considered immunized. An animal is considered currently vaccinated if the primary vaccination was administered at least 28 days prior and subsequent vaccinations have been given according to the recommended schedule. Regardless of the animal's age at the time of initial vaccination, a booster dose should be administered one year later. There is no laboratory or epidemiological evidence to support the annual or biennial administration of three-year vaccines after the initial series. Following a booster vaccination, an animal is considered currently vaccinated immediately due to the expected rapid anamnestic immune response. Dogs, cats, and ferrets that are currently vaccinated should be revaccinated immediately, kept under the owner's control, and observed for 45 days. All livestock species are susceptible to rabies, with cattle and horses being the most frequently infected. Livestock exposed to a rabid animal and currently vaccinated with a USDA-approved vaccine for that species should be revaccinated immediately and observed for 45 days. Unvaccinated livestock should be slaughtered immediately. If the owner refuses, the animal should be closely observed for six months. For unvaccinated livestock exposed to rabies, the following recommendations apply: 1. If the animal is slaughtered within seven days of being bitten, its tissues may be consumed without risk of infection, provided that liberal portions of the exposed area are discarded. Federal guidelines require that any animal exposed to rabies within eight months be rejected for slaughter. 2. Tissues or milk from a rabid animal should not be used for human or animal consumption. 3. The occurrence of multiple rabid animals in a herd or herbivore-to-herbivore transmission is rare. Therefore, restricting the rest of the herd may not be necessary if a single animal has been exposed to or infected by rabies. The translocation of terrestrial rabies reservoir species should be prohibited. The use of licensed oral vaccines for mass vaccination of free-ranging wildlife may be considered in specific situations with the approval of the state agency responsible for animal rabies control. The distribution of oral rabies vaccines should be based on scientific assessments of the target species and followed by timely analysis of surveillance data, with results shared with all stakeholders. Continuous programs for trapping or poisoning wildlife are not effective in reducing rabies reservoirs on a statewide basis. State agriculture, public health, and wildlife agencies should be consulted for planning, coordination, and evaluation of vaccination or population-reduction programs. Rabid bats have been reported in every state except Hawaii and have caused rabies in at least 40 humans in the United States. To prevent direct contact with humans, bats should be excluded from houses, public buildings, and adjacent structures. These structures should then be made bat-proof by sealing all entrances used by bats. Programs aimed at reducing bat populations to control rabies are neither feasible nor desirable.
